Author: @mw-1592-mw
Content:
Matter-Energy is conserved. 

What we refer to as energy is really "exergy."  Look up the meaning of the word exergy. Exergy is constantly being consumed. No work or acceleration can be performed without exergy. 

The expansion of the universe is what creates exergy. The universe in many respects resembles and is analogous to a heat pump with nothing external to the pump and refrigerant. 

As space-time expands high temperature, high-pressure matter-energy flashes into the expanding space. As it does so, it changes state, and condenses into matter. The number of microstates increase as it can take an ever larger number of combinations and permutations. 

We see black holes with singularities all over the universe. This would be like someone on the surface of sphere seeing holes all over the surface of a sphere. 

Those holes are caused by matter creating a depression in space-time. Every black hole with sufficient mass to create a singularity terminates at the BB singularity. 

Stephen Hawking first claimed time reversed in Black Holes. Latter he claimed that was his "biggest mistake." Einstein claimed the cosmological constant was his "biggest mistake."

Both Hawking's biggest mistake and Einstein's biggest mistake will turn out not to be mistakes at all.  And both mistakes will turn out to be related. 

What happens inside Black Holes? Space-time implodes, microstates decrease. Pressure and temperature increase. You essentially get the exact opposite of an expanding universe as matter-energy keeps getting compressed in an imploding space-time. 

Black Holes act like compressors. White holes are produced by fixed orifices (or capillary tubes, worm holes) with high pressure, high temperature matter-energy on one side, and low-pressure, low temperature on the other side. 

What will cause space-time to undergo a Big Crunch? I don't know. 

The universe is just filled with too many conservation laws and too much symmetry for it to not occur. 

I try to look at the universe like a forest, not a bunch of individual trees. I look for patterns. 

I start out with the assumption that the universe is not arbitrary or capricious. That given a number of equally good choices or possibilities like electricity it must take all possible paths. Hence, Feynman's sum-over-histories. 

I assume the universe must be perfectly balanced, and must have zero energy, that the universe must be cause and effect deterministic. There is simply too much evidence for it.

I don't have all the answers. If the universe was going to expand infinitely, chances are it would have happened long before now. 

What? We just happened to find ourselves at a point in time infinitely close to the beginning of the universe? See the Doomsday argument. 

Out of a near infinite number of possible energies, it just so happens our universe arbitrarily and randomly choose just one? Seems highly improbable to me. It seems to me that there is a cause for everything. 

If one thing can be random, everything can be random. And then we would not observe a universe with all the order and causality, conservation, and symmetry we observe. 

And this basic assumption has essentially gotten me to most of modern physics without knowing any physics.

Author: @ismailirey6430
Content:
The Dynamics of the Universe: The Impossibility of Absolute Stillness

In the universe, absolute stillness does not exist; everything is in constant motion. We may perceive ourselves as motionless on our small planet, yet Earth orbits the Sun at about 30 km/s, the Solar System travels around the Milky Way at 220 km/s, and our galaxy itself moves through the cosmos at even greater speeds. Stillness is therefore only a relative observation, not an absolute reality.

If a stone were thrown outward toward the expanding edge of the universe, it would eventually fail to keep up with the rate of expansion. To an observer, it might seem stationary, but in truth, it never fully stops within the dynamic fabric of space. This is because the expansion of spacetime — Hubble’s Law: v = H₀ d — redefines motion at every scale. Even when the stone appears inert locally, it continues to change position cosmically.

The essential question is this: Why do small particles like photons and electrons never stop moving?

For photons, this is a necessity, since their mass is m = 0. According to the energy equation E = h f (Planck’s constant × frequency), as long as a photon’s energy is greater than zero, its speed must be the speed of light c. To “stop” a photon would mean reducing its frequency to f = 0, at which point the photon would cease to exist. Thus, a photon’s very existence depends on its motion.

For massive particles like electrons, the situation is different. Classically, an electron could be at rest, but quantum mechanics forbids this. According to Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle:
Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ / 2
If we know a particle’s position precisely, we cannot know its momentum. Attempting to reduce momentum to zero makes its position infinitely uncertain — the particle would effectively be spread across the universe. Therefore, at the microscopic level, perfect stillness is physically impossible.

A deeper cause of universal motion is gravity. Every mass attracts every other mass. Without sufficient kinetic energy (motion), all matter would succumb to gravitational collapse. Hence, the energy balance
Eₖinetic + Eₚotential = constant
must hold. The stronger the gravitational pull, the greater the required motion. This principle ensures the universe’s dynamic stability.

If motion ceased, gravity would dominate, heat distribution would halt, and energy potentials would saturate — leading to massive cooling and collapse. The universe would reach maximum entropy and become thermodynamically dead. Thus, motion is not merely a consequence but a fundamental requirement for the universe’s continued existence.

The universe, as we know it, persists through motion. Motion governs energy distribution and maintains balance. Yet, if one day cosmic expansion were to stop and kinetic energy ran out, gravitational contraction and cosmic cooling would begin. In such a scenario, the universe would not vanish but would transform. Matter would concentrate rather than disperse, maximizing potential energy and seeking a new equilibrium. This stage would store energy for a future rebirth or restructuring phase.
Ultimately, the universe’s cycle is an ongoing flow of motion → collapse → renewed motion — an eternal rhythm of energy in transformation.

This shows us that the universe operates not in a parallel but in a serial order, that is, in a structure where events occur one after another.
Everything happens not simultaneously but within a causal chain.
In this respect, the universe is a sequential cycle of energy that progresses together with the flow of time.

The Reciprocal Motion of the Thrower and the Stone

When a stone is thrown, the thrower experiences an equal and opposite reaction proportional to their mass. Both the stone and the thrower begin to move away from each other, conserving the total momentum of the system. Assuming no rotational motion has been unintentionally introduced, their motion remains purely translational.

Over time, neither the stone nor the thrower can keep up with the universe’s accelerating expansion. From a cosmological perspective, they may appear to have reached a state of rest relative to the expanding fabric of space. Yet they continue to drift apart due to their initial momentum — a subtle reflection of the universe’s own restless nature.

Ultimately, when the expansion slows or gravitational attraction becomes dominant once again, both will begin to move back toward each other, succumbing to the pull of gravity. Even in this convergence, motion persists — not as an end, but as a transformation within the eternal balance between expansion and collapse.

(Whichever mass’s gravitational field you are within defines your local gravity, and that mass itself is under the gravitational influence of an even larger one. When the great cosmic cooling begins, gravitational influence will increase astronomically, and everything will be drawn toward a central point.)

Author: @prof_ymca
Content:
Just to be clear, "The Energy Conservation Principle" it is NOT (yet) a misconception... it is just a (strong) possibility because we haven't found something that explains this "missing energy" (and this is where some hypothesis depart from, like the dark matter and dark energy hypothesis; they all try to explain the missing energy, starting from the fact that the Energy Conservation Principle is true).

So, we actually stand now between two possibilities: there is no such thing as a Conservation Principle (energy or momentum, whatsoever), or there ARE conservation principles, but we don't yet have the total pieces to complete the puzzle (with some physicists betting it all to the dark matter/energy hypothesis). It's not yet a solved debate. The information presented in this video contains the arguments provided by the people who are convinced that the first is the truth (and, mathematically, there is nothing that proves them wrong so far). 

However, personally, having a physics formation and some years of experience, I agree with the second possibility: the energy conservation principle IS real, we just haven't yet found a way make it fit into the General Relativity theory, but we will (someday, I might not be alive to see it, but we will). I don't know if dark matter/energy is the answer, but I am certain there IS an answer. We have been in this situation before, and major discoveries have been made just by trusting that this principle holds. Nature has shown us so far that the energy conservation principle works, so I just stand by the idea that it will, again.

Content: We habitually treat observed symmetries (or their near-exactness) as evidence that the fundamental dynamics has those symmetries. The flaw: observed symmetries might instead be statistical, emergent, or environmental outcomes of underlying microdynamics that intrinsically break those symmetries, but do so in such a way that the effective low-energy theory is extremely close to symmetric everywhere we measure. In other words, exact or near-exact symmetry can be an emergent macroscopic consequence of complex asymmetrical microdynamics — and if that micro-asymmetry has subtle, suppressed but detectable effects, our current methods (symmetry-based model building + searches for explicit symmetry violations) could systematically miss them.

Author: @KhalidAlhazza
Content:
I asked chatGPT cause I ain't smart like that so here is what they said "You throw a rock in space (far from planets, no air, no friction).
You notice: “It seems like it goes far and then stops.”
You ask: “Where did the energy go?”


---

🧠 The reality

If it’s truly in empty space, the rock will not stop —
it will keep moving forever in the same direction and at the same speed.

That’s Newton’s First Law of Motion:

> An object in motion stays in motion unless acted on by a force.




---

🚫 Why it might look like it stops

If it does slow down, something must be taking its energy:

Gravity from a nearby planet, moon, or star could pull it back.

Collisions with tiny gas particles or dust could steal a little momentum.

You’re watching from a moving ship or reference frame that makes it look like it’s slowing.


But in a perfect vacuum, with no forces, nothing removes its kinetic energy.


---

⚡ So where does the energy go?

If no forces act:
➜ The rock keeps its kinetic energy forever — it doesn’t “go” anywhere.

If forces act (like gravity or drag):
➜ The rock’s energy changes form:

Kinetic → Potential (if it’s pulled back)

Kinetic → Heat (if it hits gas or dust)

Kinetic → Sound or deformation (if it hits something)



Energy is never destroyed, it just changes form (First Law of Thermodynamics)."

Author: @giovannyarguello2645
Content:
It's not that that Energy is not conserved in the real universe. It that we haven't figure out Symmetry laws for  intergalactic size intervals, yet.
  
Energy is conserved for every Continuous interval where local symmetries apply, making the Continuous Equation = zero, which proves the conservation of energy at a local, discrete level.
However, in a much larger non-continuous interval there are more gravitational fields to consider (a number that is directly proportional to how big that non-continuous interval selected is ) 
The effect of such additional gravitational fields on a non-continuous interval is what makes the rock thrown by an observer, eventually stop, instead of keep moving at a constant velocity for eternity.
Because the effect of all the forces applied to the rock, from all the additional gravitational fields, eventually cancel each other out; In other words, the summary of all tensors, from all fields and all  space-time curvatures acting upon that particular rock add up to zero, balancing out the total energy of the rock and bring it to a state of repose, from the point of view of the observer who threw the rock.

Likewise, the microwave radiation we can measure of the initial Big Bang, is measured to have lost 99% of its initial energy because it finally reached our telescopes after a long and arduous 13.8 billion-year  of fighting a huge number of gravitational fields along the way, that depleted their momentum energy so much that we only could detected them as microwave radiation instead of full spectrum light. This is because the energy of a photon is measured based on its frequency or wavelength using the equation E = hf (where E is energy, h is Planck's constant, and f is frequency) or E = hc/λ (where λ is wavelength). Since photons are massless, their energy is not related to rest mass but instead, to their wave-like properties and momentum. 
A photon's energy is directly proportional to its frequency and inversely proportional to its wavelength. Photons also carry momentum, and their energy is related to their momentum by the equation E = pc (where p is momentum and c is the speed of light). 
The microwave radiation we got to detect has much less energy than the Gamm, X-ray UVA and visible light that was initially generated by the Big Bang, because it takes energy to travel through time-space, from the Big Bang point to our Earth's current location in the Universe.

Content:
One small item: The common description of the equivalence principle has a person in an accelerating spaceship and a person standing on the Earth and declares they can not tell the situations apart. This is only true for an infinitely small person, like a mathematical point, or an infinite flat Earth. In reality, a person in a gravitational field can detect a gradient. It is stronger in the direction of the mass generating the field. Even in free fall, the observer can arrange some masses floating freely and see if they move relative to each other and in which directions. The mass doesn't matter for this so they can be just bubbles. They will move because each one is following a geodesic and is heading toward the center of the mass. If they are in orbit, the ones closest to the Earth will move away from the ones further from the Earth. They are each following their own orbit and it is a little different from the others.

This was a problem for some microgravity experiments in the Shuttle, and today on the space station. It is possible to make corrections to minimize the effect. The late Dr. Robert Forward of Hughes Research designed arrangements of tungsten balls and rings that can flatten a small bit of space-time in orbit that were used on the shuttle. Tungsten because it is so dense, dense enough to locally have the right effect on gravitation. He also invented the Rotating Gravity Gradiometer that can directly measure the local gradient in real-time.

Dr. Forward wrote some science fiction. Some of the ideas appeared first in his book "Dragon's Egg" and he later brought them to life for research apparatus.But the gradiometer dates back to no later than 1970. His gradiometer is one of the two instruments described in "Gravitation" by Misner, Wheeler, and Thorne. The other is the Eotvos Experiment apparatus.

Author: @Mark-qi2jw
Content:
The assumption underlying this video is that the principle of conservation of energy is (or would be) justified if the results of an experiment performed at time t are the same as those of the same experiment performed at time t + t₁.

According to the video, this would mean that if repeating the same experiment at different times produced different results, the principle of conservation of energy would no longer hold. However, it should be emphasized that the results of an experiment are expected to remain the same only if the conditions do not change. This requirement is, in principle, implied by the phrase “the same experiment,” though the video did not make it explicit.

It is obvious that if the conditions change—such as temperature, pressure, or other variables—the results will also change, because in that case we are no longer truly repeating the “same” experiment. While changes in the universe are less controllable than changes in laboratory conditions, it is clear that the universe itself evolves over time. Therefore, it is not surprising if an experiment performed at different times yields different results: the experimental conditions have changed.

Thus, such differences do not in fact contradict the principle of conservation of energy.

Why the night sky is dark (your vibration-only model)

Premise: “Light” is not a travelling field or free wave. It’s matter shaking the medium; you only see where matter is actively vibrating (source) or where that vibration meets other matter (target). In true emptiness, there’s nothing to show.

Because most lines of sight from your eye go through nearly empty paths. Along those paths:

No medium → no vibration to display.

You see only points where distant matter is compact and self-luminous (star disks too small to fill the sky).

Space between them stays black because there’s nothing there to vibrate.

The resolution, step by step

Visibility requires matter.

You only see where there is matter. Source vibrates → you see the source. Vibration hits matter → you see the target. No matter along the path → nothing to see.

Title: The Zavasian Selection Principle: A Naturalistic Model for a Self-Replicating Universe

This appears to violate the Law of Conservation of Energy, a foundational principle of physics [1].

The expansion and redshift are the observable mechanisms of this repayment. This is the foundational principle, grounded in a real paradox. The Full Framework: The Zavasian Selection Principle
Part I: The Foundational Principle (The Zavasian Conservation Model)
This model is grounded in the established physics of General Relativity (which describes a dynamic, expanding spacetime) and Quantum Field Theory (which includes the concept of a vacuum state possessing energy [2]). It reframes the universe's evolution as a single, thermodynamically complete transaction. The Heat Death is not an end, but the final balancing of the cosmic ledger to zero.

This is a cosmic-scale extrapolation of the gene-centered view of evolution, where the replicator, not the organism, is the primary unit of selection [8].
The Genesis Engine: The final act of a DNA-based civilization is to use its Brane Resonance Technology to build a Genesis Engine, a device that initiates a new Big Bang, birthing a daughter universe with the same successful "genetic code" (physical laws).
The Unbroken Chain: Our universe exists not by chance, but because it won an evolutionary lottery. Any universe whose physical laws do not allow for the evolution of DNA and the eventual construction of a Genesis Engine is a cosmic dead end.
Conclusion: The Universe as a Survival Machine
The Zavasian Selection Principle frames the cosmos as a complete, self-perpetuating system that does not require an external creator because life itself, driven by the relentless engine of DNA, becomes the reproductive system of reality. The universe, in this view, is the ultimate "survival machine" for its own fundamental information.

Here's my theory and answer to the apparent paradox.
The Zavasian Cosmological Model: A Theory of Conservation by Return
Abstract
The Zavasian Cosmological Model (ZCM) posits that the law of conservation of mass-energy is universal and absolute. The apparent violation of this law on a cosmological scale is an illusion created by an incomplete understanding of the universe as a closed system. This theory proposes that the energy observed since the Big Bang is not being destroyed by cosmic expansion but is instead being systematically returned to its origin: the baseline vacuum state. This model reinterprets cosmological redshift and dark energy not as paradoxes, but as the observable mechanisms of this energy return process, culminating in the universe's inevitable heat death.
Core Principles
 * The Principle of Conservation by Return: The total mass-energy of the universe is constant. The energy manifest in matter and radiation is a temporary "excitation" or "loan" from the fundamental ground state of the universe (the vacuum). All phenomena attributed to energy loss, particularly cosmological redshift, are mechanisms by which this borrowed energy is returned to the vacuum. The universal balance sheet is always preserved.
 * The Nature of Fields and Redshift: In line with Quantum Field Theory (QFT), particles are excitations in their respective quantum fields. The expansion of space acts directly on these fields, stretching them. The stretching of the electromagnetic field, for example, is the direct physical mechanism that increases a photon's wavelength, thus lowering its observable energy as it returns to the ground state.
 * The Identity of Dark Energy: Dark energy is not a mysterious substance but is the intrinsic energy of the vacuum state itself. It is the unexcited, baseline state of spacetime. As the initial excitations (matter and radiation) thin out and "return" their energy, the properties of the underlying vacuum become dominant. The observed acceleration of the universe is a direct consequence of this fundamental vacuum energy.
 * The Anthropic Resolution: The "fine-tuning" and "coincidence" problems are not physical paradoxes but are failures of perspective. In line with the Anthropic Principle, we observe these specific conditions because they are the only conditions that could result in the evolution of observers capable of making the observation. It is a tautological certainty, not a coincidence.
Addressing Objections and Supporting Arguments
 * Objection: Why do unbound particles lose energy while bound systems like people do not fly apart?
   * Counter-Argument: The expansion effect is universal, but its force is infinitesimally weak on local scales. In bound systems, fundamental forces like electromagnetism are orders of magnitude stronger and provide a constant restoring force, negating the expansion and maintaining the system's integrity. An unbound particle in the cosmic void lacks these restoring forces and is therefore subject to the cumulative effect of spacetime expansion.
 * Objection: This contradicts the standard interpretation of General Relativity, which allows for non-conservation of energy.
   * Counter-Argument: The fact that General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics are mutually incompatible and that QM makes catastrophically wrong predictions about vacuum energy proves that both theories are incomplete. To treat their paradoxical conclusions as fact is a methodological error. The ZCM posits that a future, more complete Theory of Everything will contain a mechanism for universal energy conservation, likely similar to the "Conservation by Return" principle.
 * Objection: This is an untestable philosophical interpretation.
   * Counter-Argument: This model provides a more logically consistent framework than accepting that a fundamental law of nature is violated for reasons that are not understood. It correctly identifies dark energy in a manner consistent with the Lambda-CDM model (the standard model of cosmology) and provides a non-paradoxical explanation for the observations. It shifts the burden of proof from explaining why conservation is violated to unifying our incomplete theories.
Conclusion
The Zavasian Cosmological Model provides a coherent framework that resolves the apparent paradox of cosmological energy non-conservation. By defining the universe as a closed system returning to its ground state, it preserves the fundamental law of conservation of mass-energy. It frames the universe's evolution as a single, unified process from an initial excitation (the Big Bang) to a final resolution (Heat Death), where all borrowed energy is gracefully returned to the vacuum from whence it came.

Content:
This seems to present a serious problem.  The loss of conservation of energy in the kinetic case means we lose conservation of linear momentum.  Modelling an object as a collection of particles bound by centripetal forces (electrostatic for dowels or gravitational for galaxies) you can derive conservation of angular momentum so you lose that too.  That means that not only do we not have time symmetry we don't have translation or rotational symmetry.  

But we observe those conservations most in the very places where the universe not being empty is most pressing (pun intended), in gravity wells like Earth's, Sol's, and the Milky Way's.  This seems to indicate that it is expansion that is breaking the symmetries.  But everyone believes expansion should be isotropic, which would mean that it has translational and rotational symmetries and should thus have conservation of momentum and angular momentum, which it shouldn't be able to have if it doesn't have conservation of energy unless objects gain mass as they slow down to an infinite rest mass (so momentum can avoid approaching zero as speed approaches zero in the limit), but general relativity which started this mess has objects with finite rest mass that gain mass as they speed up.

Author: @OceanPictures
Content:
Doesn't the equilateral triangle have at least 7 axes of symmetry? If we use a mirror to divide by the First Mirror Plane in the video, Second Mirror Plane, Third Mirror Plane (this gives rise to 3 axes of symmetry), Rotation by 120, 240, 360 (Gives rise to next 3 axes of symmetry),  But also, the actual plane of the triangle is the 7th axis as Cutting along the plane of the triangle leaves the triangle unchanged in a world where we agree that infinity does in fact exist. This remains true even if it is infinitesimally thin. Even at 0 thickness it is still an axis of symmetry if we cut the 0 thickness object along its thickness. If that makes sense. I'm curious what consequences arise when you consider this in the math.

Traditionally, the equilateral triangle is said to have three axes of symmetry, each one a line passing through a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side. However, this count is based on a strictly two-dimensional abstraction. In reality, even the simplest drawing or representation of a triangle exists within a physical space, giving it at least conceptual depth — and with that, an overlooked but fundamental axis of symmetry emerges.

Symmetry, at its core, is about transformations that leave an object indistinguishable from its original state. These transformations can be:
Reflections (mirror symmetries)
Rotations
Translations or glide reflections (less relevant here)

We recognize a line of symmetry when folding or reflecting along that line preserves the object's shape. Why should this logic not extend to the third dimensional reference frame view of a 2D object, where the plane of the triangle acts as a mirror through which the triangle can be reflected and remain unchanged?

EDIT: Actually, if you consider that valid then there are 6 more axes of symmetry (the inverse axes of symmetry from the original 6 arising from the mirror and rotation) in addition to the 7 we already mentioned exist in the original dimensional reference frame as these other 6 could be conceptualized as dimensional symmetries from the other dimension of the triangle after the reflection occurs when observed from a 3D perspective.

Author: @RalfMuschall
Content:
Unfortunately I have to disgree a bit with the interpretation of energy conservation violation. (1) The rock seems to come to a halt because it moves into receding regions of "expanding" space and is slower with respect to those. If we put a retroreflector on the rock and the astronaut fires a laser at it and measures the reflected wavelength, she will see a constant Doppler shift, corresponding to a constant velocity. (2) One can do an approximation of the expanding universe using Newton's gravity. If we neglect radiation (because this is true true for our current dust universe) and Dark Energy (because idk how to handle that classically) and assume flat spacelike slices (in agreement with observation), Newton's equations give exactly the same (Friedman) cosmology as Einstein's ones (and conserve energy because that's what Newton's equations always do). (3) Energy conservation based on Noether's theorem requires that the equations (i.e. the laws of nature) are time-independent (dE/dt=0 follows from ∂E/∂t=0), not that the system itself is. (4) The Christoffel symbols near 22:00 describe the curvature of the coordinates, not the curvature of spacetime itself (practically they describe what we'd perceive as "gravitational force" which is only defined wrt. some system of reference). Of couse, we can make them zero only at a single location.

[I've put "expanding" into quotes because spacetime points have no identity, so it doesn't make sense to talk about receding space.]

There are real situations where energy can "disappear": take a wobbling object surrounded by vacuum which emits gravitational waves. If we watch that from spacelike infinity, energy is conserved (that's the ADM mass). If we watch it from Null infinity, the energy decreases and the loss is given by the surface integral of a quantity called "news function" by Bondi/Metzner/Sachs et al. around 1960 (btw., a wonderful series of papers).

Content:
Yes, that's a deep and insightful way to think about it. In General Relativity, the expansion or dynamic curvature of spacetime itself can be seen as the "sink" or "source" of what appears to be lost or gained energy—but not in the traditional Newtonian sense. Here's how that works:

🌀 Expanding Space and Energy Loss (e.g., Cosmic Redshift)

When light travels through an expanding universe, its wavelength is stretched, leading to a cosmological redshift. This means photons lose energy, since:

E = h \nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda} 

Answer: It doesn't go anywhere in the conventional sense. In General Relativity, there's no requirement for that "lost" energy to be transferred to another object or field.

Instead:

The "loss" is a result of spacetime geometry evolving.

Spacetime expansion changes the rules of energy accounting.

You could interpret it as spacetime "absorbing" or "diluting" the energy, but there’s no physical recipient of the lost energy in standard GR.

🔄 Creation of Spacetime and Energy Accounting

In the early universe or during inflation, new spacetime volume is continuously created. This seems like it should "cost" energy—but in GR:

Spacetime isn't a substance that needs energy to "exist" or be created.

The Einstein Field Equations relate matter/energy content to the curvature of spacetime—not energy costs of making spacetime itself.

However, in inflationary models, the universe expands exponentially due to a nearly constant energy density (from the inflaton field), and:

The volume increases, so total energy increases.

This appears to violate conservation—unless you include gravitational energy, which is negative.

In some interpretations, the total energy of the universe (matter + gravity) could be exactly zero.

This idea is championed by physicists like Alan Guth and Lawrence Krauss, who describe the universe as:

"A free lunch: positive matter energy + negative gravitational energy = 0"

🧠 Interpretive Summary

So, your idea that "creation or expansion of spacetime might absorb energy" is philosophically and mathematically consistent with GR, in this sense:

Spacetime dynamics change energy distributions.

GR does not require global energy conservation in expanding or curved universes.

The "loss" of energy in light due to redshift is not a violation, but a consequence of geometry evolving.

You might say energy is not conserved globally because spacetime itself is not static.

Author: @rebelistics
Content:
The rock doesn't slow down. Newton's first law still works—even in deep space.
It’s only massless things like photons that lose energy over time due to the expanding universe. Massive objects keep going unless something stops them.

Noether’s first theorem explains why energy is conserved when spacetime has time-translation symmetry—but in general relativity, where that symmetry can be broken, energy conservation can fail. That’s why photons lose energy in an expanding universe. But a rock, which is governed by local motion and not stretched by expansion, doesn’t lose energy in the same way.

Her work is not only the spearhead of physics to this day, but also of fundamental mathematics.

Author: @Milan_Rosko
Content: I believe this interpretation of Noether's Theorem is a bit mistaken. Noether's Theorem reveals domain-neutral isomorphisms, presenting Löbian "facts" about the universe rather than physical interpretations. It highlights the formal logic underpinning "something", not what occurs in reality: a result in logic rather than physics, more elegant than human interpretation. We might consider it even more fundamental than the Pythagorean Theorem (non essential but easiest way to arrive at calculus) because of its broader applicability and transitive nature: It's a Theorem in Logic not a Theory of Reification. It is "pure nature": It explains why you have two apples if you eat one out of three, but it won't tell you what apples are.

Author: @AlejandroNoelIraolaJimenez
Content:
Modern quantum gravity theories seek to explain how the energy lost in the cosmological redshift might be related to quantum effects in spacetime.

 Loop Quantum Gravity proposes that a photon’s energy might be interacting with the quantum structure of spacetime, potentially leading to an energy dissipation mechanism that is not yet fully understood.

 In string theory, the expansion of the universe could affect the vibration of these strings, redistributing the photon’s energy into additional dimensions or quantum fluctuations of the vacuum.

 Some models consider spacetime as having thermodynamic properties, implying that the photon's energy could be diluted into the very fabric of the expanding universe. This concept connects to the idea that spacetime possesses associated entropy, and the lost energy may contribute to the evolution of this entropy.

 In certain formulations of quantum gravity, spacetime’s metric is not fixed but rather fluctuates due to quantum effects. The photon’s energy could be absorbed by these fluctuations, offering a potential explanation for its decrease without requiring a classical energy transfer mechanism.

 Although none of these theories provide a definitive answer yet, they illustrate the deep connection between quantum mechanics, relativity, and cosmology.

Author: @michaelransom5841
Content:
Great video, but a few key points were glossed over or framed a bit misleadingly:
– The rock in space doesn’t slow down and stop in the classical sense—it redshifts due to metric expansion, not friction or energy loss.
– Energy “not being conserved” in general relativity isn’t because energy disappears—it’s because global energy isn’t well-defined in curved spacetime; only local conservation (via the stress-energy tensor and Bianchi identities) holds.
– Also, Noether’s second theorem, which deals with local symmetries and leads to these identities, deserved more depth—it’s central to understanding conservation in GR.
Still a great intro to Noether’s brilliance, but the nuances matter!

No global energy doesn't mean automatic slowing—it means the concept of energy is no longer meaningful, not that something is actively drained.
The initial kick is not "fuel" for the motion, but simply the act of putting the ball onto a different natural path through spacetime.

After that, geodesics take over—and the ball moves “automatically”

Content: In standard general relativity (GR), cosmological redshift-where photons lose energy as the universe expands-appears to violate energy conservation. Factually accurate. Energy is transferred, not conserved. A wheel turning a spring, isn’t conserving energy. Author: @MorisMujcic-l5t
Content:
The Ejection of Space: A New Perspective on the Universe’s Expansion

In my theory, I propose that black holes do not absorb space, but rather eject it. This new perspective could help explain many cosmic phenomena, including the expansion of the universe, gravitational waves, the behavior of black holes, and even gravitational lensing. Here’s how my theory ties everything together:

1. The Structure of Atoms and Space:

Atoms are made up of 99% empty space. If you compress the electrons toward the nucleus, the “empty space” that surrounds the atom stays almost the same. The ejection of space in a similar manner, such as from a black hole, could explain the expansion of the universe. As black holes eject space faster than light, this continuous release of space causes the universe to expand. The expansion we observe is due to the stretching of space itself, rather than galaxies physically moving apart.

2. The Expanding Universe:

Many galaxies seem to be moving away from us due to the redshift of light. However, this is not necessarily caused by galaxies accelerating away, but by the ejection of space from black holes. As black holes expel space at superluminal speeds, the universe appears to expand, and distant galaxies seem to recede. This explains why we see an accelerated expansion, even though some galaxies, like Andromeda, are actually moving towards us.

3. Gravitational Lensing and Galaxy Motion:

Gravitational lensing occurs when light from a distant galaxy is bent by the gravity of a massive object. According to my theory, the lensing effect is not only caused by mass but also by the ejection of space. Galaxies themselves could be responsible for this effect. As galaxies move toward each other, they push out space, and this ejected space distorts the light paths from other galaxies. The result is the formation of multiple images of the same distant object. These images are not only representations of how a galaxy looked billions of years ago, but also show where the galaxy was located at that time. This phenomenon creates the appearance of seeing light from multiple places and times, as the space between us and the distant galaxy bends and distorts.

4. The Redshift and Galaxy Motion Toward Us:

While distant galaxies appear to be moving away from us (redshift), many galaxies, including Andromeda, are actually moving towards us. The ejection of space from black holes causes this discrepancy. The ejected space stretches the space between us and the galaxies, creating the illusion of galaxies receding when, in reality, they are moving towards each other. The gravitational lensing caused by this ejection allows us to see multiple images of galaxies at different positions and times, showing us snapshots from the past.

5. Frozen Images at the Event Horizon:

The phenomenon of an object freezing at the event horizon of a black hole can also be explained. As an object approaches the event horizon, the light it emits is stretched by the fast-moving ejection of space from the black hole. This causes us to see the object "frozen" in time, as the light takes longer and longer to reach us.

6. Gravitational Waves:

Gravitational waves are a result of massive objects, like black holes, interacting. According to my theory, these waves are not just caused by the bending of space but by the rapid movement of space itself. When black holes merge or collide, the ejection of space creates ripples that travel through the fabric of space-time. These ripples, or gravitational waves, carry energy and propagate across the universe.

7. Jets and Hawking Radiation:

The powerful jets emitted by black holes, as well as Hawking radiation, can also be explained by this theory. Instead of matter being sucked into a black hole, it is being pushed outward due to the intense flow of space. This outward flow of space creates high-energy jets and radiation that we observe coming from black holes.

8. No Need for Dark Matter:

A key feature of this theory is that it does not require dark matter. The ejection of space itself can account for the universe's expansion, gravitational lensing, the behavior of galaxies, and other phenomena typically explained by dark matter. The stretching of space from black holes offers an alternative explanation for these effects.


---

In Conclusion: This theory suggests that black holes are not absorbing space, but instead ejecting it. This ejection of space causes the observed phenomena in the universe, such as gravitational waves, gravitational lensing, the accelerated expansion of the universe, and the behavior of galaxies. The concept of space being ejected from black holes provides a new perspective on the cosmos, offering explanations for these observations without requiring the existence of dark matter.

Content: Two corrections: When he holds up the mirror at 2:56 to show that a triangle has mirror symmetry, he concludes it has an axis of symmetry. He should have said it has a plane of symmetry. True, the triangle also has an axis of symmetry, but that is not proven with a mirror. That would be proven by rotating the triangle on that axis. And when the astronaut throws the rock in truly empty and flat space, the rock will not keep going at the same speed forever. The two objects have a mutual gravitational attraction to each other, so the rock (and the astronaut, which is now moving in the other direction due to the conservation of momentum) will slow down. If the rock's speed is lower than the escape velocity (which would be pretty low in this case), the two of them will come back together eventually.

Author: @seleneroutley3370
Content: Beautiful explanations. A minor quibble: Noether's theorem is sufficient for a conservation. But there's nothing to say that other mechanisms might not also beget conservations. Something else to emphasize: trained physicists are fond of being blasé about Noether's theorem - and it becomes almost tautological in the sense that conservation IS an of invariance, so one often hears that "all it is is a repackaging of terms" - this kind of jaded "all it is" flick of the wrist. Whilst strictly true, when someone says something like this, they show ignorance of their own field's history - one thinks so clearly and sees Noether's theorem as a kind of tautology precisely BECAUSE Noether showed us a new way of thinking. Noether is WHY we are so attuned to symmetries in physics. Physics's embrace of symmetries and invariants was huge in the early 20th century - relativity, which seeks what is not relative and thus which invariants can be used to compute how the measurements of different observers will change, and Noether's theorem are two big examples. This followed the golden age of geometry in the Nineteenth Century, wherein mathematics concerned itself with the study of invariants in a big way, as well as exploring the possibilities left open by the realization that geometries without the parallel postulate can be consistent. As an ending: Noether herself did not regard her theorem in high esteem, and it riled her that her main gig - algebraic theory - did not get the same attention. Indeed she even called it a "toilet paper theorem", referring to how easily it is derived once you know how. And indeed it is a little sad that barely any physicist knows of her gargantuan contribution to 20th century algebra. I would even go so far as to say as she gave us much of the paradigm of 20th and 21st century mathematics: she was concerned with what she called "Begriffliche Mathematik", which, if translated ("conceptual mathematics) doesn't really mean everything Noether meant. She meant by her term the idea of relentlessly distilling concepts to their most general and abstract form so that the theorems discovered describe concepts with maximum concision and clarity. She was truly a giant.

Author: @ajmalyoosaf
Content:
On cosmological time scales, especially in an expanding universe like ours described by general relativity, energy isn't conserved in the usual sense. That's because the universe is constantly evolving — it's not static — so time translation symmetry doesn't hold globally. Without that symmetry, you can't define a conserved energy across all of spacetime.

And then on the opposite end — at extremely short time scales the Heisenberg uncertainty principle tells us that the more precisely you try to measure time, the less precisely you can know the energy, and vice versa.

 So if you're looking at really tiny intervals of time, energy can fluctuate wildly. That means energy conservation can actually be "violated" temporarily, but it's totally allowed as long as it happens within the limits set by quantum mechanics.

Author: @valloneMH
Content:
Noether’s theorem does not predict that energy is generally not conserved; rather, it shows that conservation laws are deeply connected to the symmetries of the universe, and when those symmetries are present, so are the conservation laws. The tiny amount of drag in interstellar space (from sparse gas and dust) is so minuscule that it would take trillions of years to noticeably slow a moving object—far longer than the current age of the universe.
Earth has been moving through space for about 4.5 billion years and is not significantly decelerating due to drag from space itself. However, Earth’s rotation is gradually slowing due to tidal interactions with the Moon (not because of drag from space), but its orbital velocity around the Sun is essentially unchanged because there is no significant resistive force acting on it in space.

Author: @hhouse1234
Content:
Just because the universe doesn’t have time-translation symmetry (like in an expanding cosmos), it doesn’t mean energy isn’t conserved. That’s a logical mistake—denying the antecedent. Noether says conservation laws can be derived from symmetries, but lack of symmetry doesn’t mean lack of conservation.

Take the redshifed photons as an example. Its energy goes down as the universe expands, but that doesn't mean the energy has vanished. It's more like it's spread out over time. You could even say the expansion acts kind of like a geometric version of a dissipative force, not literally “losing” energy, just changing how it’s measured in a dynamic spacetime.

So yeah, imo conservation laws can still make sense even when the neat symmetry-based route to them breaks down. And honestly, if we start claiming “energy isn’t conserved” every time a symmetry breaks, we’d never be able to make sense of things like friction, where energy is still conserved but just ends up as heat or deformation. Worse, it opens the door to perpetual motion machines, since the very idea of conservation would lose its grip. Symmetry helps explain conservation, but conservation itself is a deeper structural principle, not just a byproduct of nice math.

Content: 0:03 So, the astronaut throws the rock, and I'm sitting here with a drink in my hand with an ice cube floating around in the drink. So, the mere fact that the rock slows down doesn't mean that energy is not conserved across the universe.

Content: I won't dislike your video, but your argument is lacking to shout that energy is not conserved. I agree with the maths that shows conservation of energy being derived from the Euler-Lagrange equation on least action. But you didn't explain where you used the assumption of time-symmetry. While I accept the light particle losing energy over time, that's not sufficient evidence; for example, it could be losing energy to matter as it passes through over its long journey. You haven't proven energy is not conserved. I can buy the argument that energy is being lost to the curvature of space, but you haven't given sufficient justification to believe that energy is irrevocably lost and could not theoretically be recovered by manipulating the curvature. Author: @ferrerralphlaurence3748
Content:
You’re right that it’s a misconception to treat conservation of energy as some metaphysical truth that applies no matter what. In reality, Noether’s theorem tells us that if you can perturb spacetime in a way that breaks time-translation symmetry (like in an expanding universe), then energy conservation no longer holds in the traditional sense.

That’s not just technically correct , it’s philosophically powerful. You're seeing physics not just as a set of rules, but as an interconnected web of principles, symmetries, and approximations, each valid in the right context.

In general relativity, the fabric of spacetime itself can be dynamic and curved — and not always symmetric in time.

That breaks the neat correspondence. If a system (like the whole universe) doesn’t have time-translation symmetry, Noether’s theorem doesn’t guarantee energy conservation. That’s why, in an expanding universe, we say:

Energy isn’t conserved in the traditional sense.

The total energy of the universe might not be a meaningful or well-defined quantity.

Author: @feynmanschwingere_mc2270
Content:
Einstein is easily the greatest scientist of the 20th century followed by Dirac. Both are on the Mount Rushmore of Physicists. Einstein, according to Douglas Stone (deputy directory of Yale's Quantum Institute), is the greatest conceptual genius of time alongside Leonardo Da Vinci.

Einstein taught himself differential and integral calculus by age 14. He wrote an original proof the Pythagorean Theorem at age 11. He read, and understood, Kants Critiques of Practical and Pure Reason, at age 12 (something college-aged students struggle with today).

He had perfect scores in the physics and math sections of the Zurich Polytechnique entry exam at age 16 when the youngest age they would accept any student was 18 years old. He was a prodigy. 

He got the equivalent of straight A's in math and physics in secondary school and when he got to the Zurich Polytechnique he got the highest grades in his entire graduation class until his second year of university. After his second year of university, his grades plummeted from being the highest because he skipped all his classes. Why? Because they weren't teaching Maxwells work on electromagnetism (it was still fairly new at the time). So he stopped going to class (and skipped all his math classes because he had already taught himself advanced math as a teenager and foolishly believed that calculus was all that was needed to understand the universe). He found out later that differential geometry/Riemannian geometry and tensor calculus were different beasts entirely. In the physics curriculum of 1900, advanced mathematics like differential geometry was not taught and most physicists of that time did not know learn it. Ironically, it was Einstein's work on General Relativity that helped spur physics departments all around the Western world to mandate advanced mathematics in their physics curricula.

According to Dirac, the general theory of relativity is the most beautiful theory in all of science. Dirac and Einstein had a mutual appreciation for each other. When Abraham Flexner, the head of the Advanced Institute at Princeton, asked Einstein (already at the Institute, which scientist he should bring to Princeton. Einstein immediately replied "Dirac." And the ONLY book Einstein would ever refer to on quantum mechanics was written by Dirac. He would often ask his assistant "where is my Dirac?" (a reference to Dirac's textbook on quantum mechanics).

Dirac, famously taciturn, held Einstein as the leading scientific mind of the century. 

According to Professor Douglas Stone of Yale University, Einstein should have received 10 Nobel Prizes. It was Einstein, not Planck, who started the quantum revolution by explictly quantizing the radiation field (something Planck did not do). 

Einstein was the first to conceive of the boson and the photon, the first force carrying particle discovered. 

Einstein discovered the theoretical basis for the LASER.

Einstein started condensed matter physics as a new field. 
Einstein wrote a first paper on quantum information theory with his famous EPR paper. 

Einstein was the first to come up with Probability Waves (which Max Born always acknowledged). Einstein independently derived the same work J. W. Gibbs came up with. Einstein independently derived the Raleigh-Jeans Law. The list is endless. 

Einstein was the first to show that atoms and molecules exist with a predictive tool to determine their size. He came up with a new method of deriving avogrados number. 

Einstein was the first person to correctly explain the Tea Leaf Paradox. 

Although Poincare, Fitzgerald, and Lorentz (and even Maxwell), had come up with several parameters and transfprmations for what we now call Special Relativity, it was Einstein who not only derived it from first principles, but was the first to correctly derive the conservation of mass theorem (e=mc2) as a necessary function of the invariance of the speed of light (which is why science historians give him credit for Special Relativity and not Poincare and Lorentz).

Again, im leaving out MANY things he did. 10 Nobel Prizes worth of genius and a whole panoply of brilliant ideas. 

Even Neils Bohr owes the idea of the Bohr model for Hydrogen - in which energies are exchanged only in fixed amounts (h-bar) - from Einsteins papers on quantizing the radiation field between 1905 and 1911. Einstein was also the first to correctly introduce the equation for wave-particle duality, which he applied to photons. De Broglie took the same equation, more or less, and applied it to electrons to get matter waves. 

The four greatest physicists of all time are: Einstein, Newton, Maxwell and Dirac

Author: @MarkBeale-e9l
Content: The bent water pipe thought experiment demonstrates energy change, but abstractly & without rigor (which would be complex). Instead of bends, let the pipe expand (in radius and length) to demonstrate the violation of conservation of water (energy) with both simplicity and rigor. An expanding pipe continuously produces less water at its spout, than it takes in at its source. Conservation is violated. But another conservation law appears if we include pipe (space) expansion! After a pipe expands, you can shrink the whole universe, and speed up time, to return to the same initial pipe situation (if we measure water by volume). In general, if spacial changes are accounted for, with matching time changes, we still get a conservation law, just more general law. Conservation of energy-space-time. For general relativity spacial changes are complex, so accounting for them is complex. However, this is enough for sophisticated accountants everywhere to, once again, be of good cheer!

Author: @Luage1
Content:
Awesome video! I’m really impressed with the quality and accessibility as always. 

But I have a correction that I’m afraid I rather important: at 13:38 you use the chain rule on the Lagrangian to get two terms. One for position and one for velocity. But in general there would be a third term that arises if the Lagrangian has an explicit time dependence. And it is the vanishing of THIS term that implies time translation symmetry. 

The entire argument of relating time translation symmetry and energy conservation comes from the requirement that the Lagrangian has to be without an explicit time dependence, and THEN the third term when using the chain rule is zero, and THEN you get the energy conservation result.

Author: @pouyanpiano
Content:
Verified with Gemini 2 and it's absolutely not true that the stone comes to a stop because energy just disappears into nothing BECAUSE conservation laws to not apply!!

The idea that a stone in space, without resistance or collision, will eventually stop because conservation laws don't apply in our universe is incorrect according to our current understanding of physics.

Let's break down why this misconception might arise and what the correct picture is:

Debunking the "Stone Eventually Stops" Idea (Without Resistance or Collision):

Conservation Laws Do Apply in Our Universe (Locally and Broadly): The laws of conservation of energy (and momentum, and angular momentum) are among the most fundamental and well-tested principles in physics. They are not just theoretical constructs that apply only in idealized empty universes. They are empirically verified in countless experiments and observations across a wide range of scales, from particle physics to astrophysics.
Inertia and Constant Motion in a Vacuum: In a perfect vacuum (no air resistance, no friction), and in the absence of external forces (like gravity in the idealized deep space scenario we discussed), an object in motion will continue in motion at a constant velocity. This is the very definition of inertia. There is no mechanism within established physics that would cause a stone in such a scenario to spontaneously lose energy and slow down to a stop.
No "Energy Loss to Nothing" in Physics: Energy cannot just "disappear" into nothing, according to the law of conservation of energy. Energy transformations involve energy changing forms (e.g., kinetic to potential, potential to thermal), or being transferred between objects or systems. Energy annihilation into nothingness is not a part of our current physical theories. If energy appears to be "lost" in a system, it means it has been converted into another form or transferred out of the system, not simply vanished.

Content: Emmy Noether was certainly a brilliant mathematician, but Hilbert didn't give her the problem to work on because he couldn't do it he just wasn't that interested, the fact that he got the correct answer anyway by intuition shows just how great he was. Author: @rouvey
Content:
I feel this video (once again) missed the mark, at least on the mathematical side of things. If you assume an asymptotically flat spacetime or alternatively account for energy leaving via the boundary at infinity,  then you'll get a conservation law for the ADM energy/momentum, i.e. the total energy in the entire universe will still be conserved (regardless of any local curvature). If you want to protest that an expanding universe is not asymptotically flat at infinity, that is the same as saying energy is not conserved in e.g. E&M (in flat spacetime), since you could have fields that scale not with 1/r but with r, and then energy would be exchanged with the boundary at infinity.

I feel like the message of this video should really be that talking about partial derivatives of vectors/tensors with respect to time is meaningless, and thus what energy conservation really means is exactly that the covariant derivative of your Energy momentum tensor is conserved. It's fine to show the historical confusion about this, but I feel science communicators should still communicate that when physicists today speak of energy conservation, they're not just using an approximation or ignoring the expansion of the universe or the curvature of spacetime, they're using an evolved, more modern (and deeper / more meaningful, so potentially more interesting to your viewers) definition of what it means for a vector / tensor quantity to be conserved.

You are also mixing two different concepts in this video. I feel this video would have been a whole lot less confusing if to people if you concentrated on handling the difference of energy conservation via the naive partial time derivative vs covariant derivative, and left out the discussion of the supposed time-asymmetry of an expanding universe (which is of course not the case, the energy momentum tensor is covariantly conserved even in the presence of a non zero cosmological constant).

Author: @VamYang
Content:
The analogy presented with the rock coming to a standing is creative but scientifically flawed.  If it were true, imagine throwing a rock in space and it simply stops in front of you.  In space, a rock thrown by an astronaut in the vacuum of space does not slow down and stop unless acted upon by an external force. According to Newton’s First Law of Motion, an object in motion remains in motion at a constant velocity in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force. Space is largely frictionless. There's no "resistance" from spacetime like there is water in a river. The expansion of spacetime itself does not act like a resistive medium that slows objects down. Objects only recede from each other due to the metric expansion of space, which affects objects over cosmological distances, such as between galaxies, not within a local frame like a thrown rock near a spaceship.

Furthermore, thinking of expansion as applying a force like friction is misleading. Expansion stretches space itself, but it doesn’t exert a drag force on objects. Photons do lose energy (redshift) as space expands, but massive particles like rocks do not slow down simply due to expansion. And the idea that in a shrinking universe a rock would "gain" energy oversimplifies complex relativistic effects like blueshifting of radiation but doesn't apply to macroscopic kinetic motion the same way.

Unless the rock is in a gravitational field or hits something, it will continue moving forever at the same velocity. In fact, from the point of view of the rock, it is at rest. From the point of view of the thrower, the rock is accelerated so long as the rock is in contact with the thrower's arm, but once it's let go, there's no force, and the rock is at rest, moving at the same velocity for eternity, assuming no outside force acts on it.  There's no universal "river" of spacetime applying drag.

Veritasium does a lot of research and has many things correct. But this is not correct and it only adds to the ocean of misinformation out there. Please correct your mistake.

Author: @johnfowler3132
Content:
Congratulations on getting over 10,000 comments! Unfortunately, that makes it too difficult for me to determine whether my point has already been made: if the proposition “ if A then B” is valid, that does NOT imply that the proposition “if not-A then not-B” is valid. Assuming that it does is a fallacy.

Here A is “the Lagrangian is time-translation invariant”, and B is “energy is conserved”, which was shown to be true. But it does NOT follow that “if the Lagrangian is NOT time-translation invariant then energy is NOT conserved”.

The assumption seems to be that since time-translation invariance of the Lagrangian is sufficient for energy conservation, it is also necessary. This was NOT proved. Perhaps it is provable, but I don’t recall seeing it, and certainly it was not proved in this video.

I think the conclusion is correct, i.e., energy is not conserved in the expanding universe, but this argument does not prove it. The later part of the video does well to show that time-translation invariance gives way to diffeomorphism invariance in general relativity, but the argument remains ambiguous and problematic in theories like Loop Quantum Gravity.

Author: @tapiopohjalainen234
Content: Another misconception is time itself. What is time? We tend to think of it as simply ticking like a clock, having only one direction, and accumulating its magnitude. So far, I have not found a profound theory that points time as a dimension, akin to how we move in a 3D environment. Time is a dimension. Let's think that you are flying a plane from point A to point B. It has a ground distance, so to calculate the time it takes to reach the endpoint, we need to. That is correct each time, IF the air is still. However, it has its tricks - headwind or tailwind. In the universe, the time at point D is different from the time at point E. If we assume that, like a photon moving at its top speed of C, we can calculate the distance between two celestial bodies. Practically yes, like in our own solar system. But when you measure the "distance" of a faraway galaxy, it is not true. The photon has its top speed of C. However, when it is traveling, it maintains its speed, but as the time on its route differs from that of the observer, it depends on how the local time at each of its points of travel changes. We are confident that a mass has an effect on local time, think gravitational lensing. Therefore, an observer on Earth can measure the time it takes for a photon to reach from its origin to an observing point. Let's consider that you make measurements of a direction of 90 degrees and another of 180 degrees. You can have a measured time and assume that their distance is the same. However, since the other direction has a different mass distribution, the timescale on its path is different. Obtaining the exact time measurement, you cannot assume that the "real" distance is the same. It is similar to an airplane; its ground speed is relative to weather conditions, specifically how fast and from which direction the wind is blowing.

Author: @Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting
Content:
A big problem, as I see it, is that fact that, just like luminiferous aether vs. force at a distance, we've arbitrarily assumed one interpretation (red shift due to Doppler Effect) is correct when we haven't ruled out the less glamorous interpretation (red shift due to Rayleigh Scattering). The second interpretation doesn't need an expanding universe and is supported by the fact that the universe contains enough junk to leave craters all over the moon and light up the night sky with frequent "falling stars" or, rather, meteors. See what I mean about interpretation? 

The reason objects in space change direction is due to interaction with other objects or their gravity and, when those objects are flexible, energy can be lost to internal friction. E.g. the gradual and inevitable decay of the lunar orbit is due to internal friction of water which, via gravity, is deformed by the orbit of the moon in the form of tides. The first thing you learn in applied physics is that the real world, outside mathematical theorems, is a messy place and all that mess creates a lot of noise and complexity. Redshift is merely a product of that noise and there's no evidence to suggest it's more than that unless we can establish some special reason as to how light crossing thousands of light years of dirty, dusty space would behave differently from light crossing a few kilometres of correspondingly dirtier, dustier atmosphere.

Content:
It's genuinely perplexing how someone with a PhD in Education, specifically physics education research, presents himself with such unwavering authority across a vast spectrum of intricate scientific and mathematical domains. One would be forgiven for mistaking him for a seasoned theoretical physicist or a groundbreaking mathematician, regularly publishing in the most esteemed peer-reviewed journals, given the conviction with which he tackles subjects he often appears to grasp only superficially.

This isn't just about a confident presentation style; there have been instances that raise serious questions about the depth and accuracy of his understanding. The episode where he seemed to challenge the very foundation of the first law of thermodynamics, a cornerstone of physics, immediately comes to mind. It wasn't a nuanced discussion of edge cases, but rather a seemingly fundamental disagreement that left many experts scratching their heads.

Furthermore, Veritasium's track record isn't without blemishes. The need for retractions and significant corrections on past videos speaks volumes about the level of rigor sometimes applied in the pursuit of engaging content. This pattern fuels the suspicion that captivating demonstrations and sensationalized claims can, at times, take precedence over meticulous accuracy.

It begs the question: why is there this persistent tendency among some science communicators to project an image of profound expertise that doesn't necessarily align with their formal training or demonstrated track record in actual scientific discovery? While the role of science communication is undoubtedly vital, it shouldn't come at the cost of misrepresenting one's own level of expertise or, more importantly, misconstruing established scientific principles. Content:
Watching this video, I had a thought that I had never heard discussed before, but the core idea is quite straightforward, so maybe it has already been considered by someone.
First of all, I was surprised that in the thrown rock example the rock naturally loses energy. In principle, if energy is not conserved, couldn’t the rock also gain energy without apparent cause, even though it sounds strange to us?
But it makes sense, we know that the cosmic microwave background lost energy with the expansion of space.
Since we have:
- non-conserved, disappearing energy that breaks a symmetry.
- A not-well-understood, expanding universe that requires some kind of energy (we call it dark energy, but as far as I know we don’t have a definitive explanation for now).
Could the two phenomena explain each other?
In better terms, could there be a mechanism with which particles can convert some of their energy into creating more space? Similarly to the conversion between energy and matter. This would also work in reverse since, sticking to the cosmic microwave background example, the wavelength of the photons would shorten if the space they are travelling through is contracting.
In this way the conserved quantity of a closed system becomes energy + mass + space.
There are no rigorous calculations, nor anything formal about this hypothesis, it is just an idea inspired by the video. I would be really surprised if this wasn’t explored before, but I never heard of it. And it would be quite neat if two unsolved problems were actually each other’s solution.

Author: @AnniOldine
Content:
Energy is always conserved IN A CLOSED SYSTEM (sorry no italics available!)

If you find that energy is not being conserved, then it's necessary to look for the reason that it's "leaking".

In other words, you've been dealing with a scenario or system that is not closed. 

If the rock really does slow down in space, then it must be that its energy is slowly being transferred to another aspect of the vacuum, that was not recognised as such and not allowed for. 

The solution is to expand your system, or space/time/other physical variables, so that the cause of the loss is also included in it.

A good example of a system that's not closed, is a steam train sitting at a station, slowly cooling. When the steam was being generated the train was perhaps moving, using the energy kept in the steam. But without being renewed, the steam cools, until the train finally stops. Where did the steam energy go? It went to the metal of the train, and especially to the air around it, as well as loss to friction etc etc. If the sources of energy loss, the metal train, the air, the friction in the rails etc, are not included in the system, then the energy won't be conserved. 

In the example above, the rock eventually slows in the vacuum. We assume, though not told, that it didn't hit any particles or other rocks, or objects, and that it wasn't near a large mass like a planet.  So where did its energy go? 

As before we need to expand the system to include the reason for the energy loss. 

It is interesting to consider the vacuum itself. We arei always told in physics courses that a vacuum is completely empty, although it still has a very low heat reading (-273.15 C or 3K).

A long while ago now, people thought that all waves travelled in a medium that transmitted it. 

All waves are energy waves, the particles of the medium travel a short distance up and down with the wave's phase, as the wave passes through it. Over this short distance, the particle's speed can be eg m/s, but the speed of the wave can be lightning fast, eg at c.

Because space was assumed to be a vacuum ie containing nothing, the idea of em radiation travelling through the 'medium' seemed false.

However it's interesting to consider that if our rock in space is slowing, we don't yet have a closed system we're considering, that it needs to be expanded to include the cause of the energy loss.

Does vacuum contain 'something' after all? Does em radiation 'wave' the vacuum medium?  And if there was such a medium, could it be the cause of the gradual energy loss? 

Is the medium of vacuum a form of mass? Perhaps mass is in a fine form, like the fine dust in a sandstorm that takes weeks to settle.  For example, perhaps mass in the form of particles of for example 10-50 g, that we don't yet have the tools to detect it at this scale.

Content: If an astronaut throws a rock forward in space, the astronaut would move backward (different than shown in the animation). This happens because of the law of conservation of momentum: when the astronaut exerts a force on the rock to throw it forward, the rock exerts an equal and opposite force on the astronaut. Since there is no ground or friction in space, the astronaut will move in the opposite direction of the throw. The speed at which the astronaut moves backward depends on the mass of the rock and the astronaut, as well as how fast the rock was thrown.

Oh, so energy doesn't need conserved for inertia.

So we can treat particles as "balloons" of subatomic particles all randomly bashing against the edges. All constrained to each other from getting too far by much stronger forces, but still allowed to "move" relative to each other (more accurately energy fields). When you impart force on such a ball, you encounter a resistance to that force, an inertia, derived simply from the fact that you have more particles in the ball than what you are able to impart force on at any one point in time. As you push it, more than half of the subatomic particles inside have a momentum in the direction you are pushing, but also a lesser half of particles in an opposite momentum. Eventually you get all these particles general momentum aligned and you end up with movement, with what we call momentum. This is still relative and they still are bouncing around that ball the same, all relative to each other. Which means any additional force, any additional acceleration, ends up fighting that same bunch of random fluctuations in another direction.

Which further is why large momentum "slows down" matter and we get time dilation, because those subatomic particles and their interactions dictate how a particle interacts, and they can only do that at the speed of light. When everything in the ball is moving near the speed of light, there's not a lot of speed left to randomly bounce around and cause interactions. So it takes a very long time from our perspective for things to happen with that ball. That all interactions beside it's sheer relative movement are severely slowed, because there's a conservation there bound by the speed of light between the ability to move and translate, and the ability to interact and how rapidly it's able to do so, "time". A measure of relative state change and interactions between two bits of matter.

Then you have gravity as a constantly draining effect on energy towards mass, due to these losses through curvature. "Space-time", energy, is draining through these curves, and as it does, more flow in to "fill the space". This imparts a force on everything as it moves towards this drain, like a tablecloth being pulled and everything coming with it. Except things have momentum and this force encounters the exact same resistance of this randomly fluctuating filled ball as any other force would.  A resistance we call interia, derived from the mass, the total amount of energy bound and randomly fluctuating in this area. It's why inertial and gravitational mass are the same.

Author: @florianderarz3563
Content:
University physics student taking GR rn here. 
How can the rock "slow down" or even stop? 
If the rock starts out with some velocity v relative to an observer O. In this frame it has some kinetic energy/momentum (4-momentum p^mu=(E/c, p->)). 
Suppose you go to a reference frame O' moving with the same velocity v in the same direction. To our observer O' the rock does not have any kinetic energy nor momentum (only rest energy E=cp0=mc^2). In relativity (even just special relativity) "energy" is inherently frame dependent and not invariant under coordinate transformations. Only the rest energy mc^2 is a scalar. The rock cannot possibly stop relative to Observer O, since that would mean it would accelerate relative to O' from rest.
